extracted.subtask_description: Advice for authors preparing machine-learning conference submissions (ICML-style), distilled from recurring reviewer feedback; focuses on writing, structure, and technical presentation to reduce common reviewer objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision in wording and claims is essential; avoid vague or imprecise statements that leave room for reviewer confusion or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness helps reviewers quickly grasp contributions; avoid unnecessary verbosity or long, winding explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complex sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler sentences to improve readability and reduce the chance that reviewers will misparse technical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent phrasing in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistent phrasing in technical writing — varying word choice for entertainment value confuses readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same terms for the same concepts throughout the paper; don't synonymize technical terms for stylistic variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: open with context then present a surprising insight
rubrics_metrics.description: For unfamiliar ideas, open with universally accepted context, then present a surprising insight that builds logically from that foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not open with vague claims like "coverage of the space is important" without first giving the reader prior context that makes that claim meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague hedging in the introduction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hedging language weakens perceived significance; state clear, specific motivations and stakes instead of broad, imprecise claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context before introducing specialized concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Always provide context before introducing specialized concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce background and intuition so that reviewers unfamiliar with a subtopic can follow subsequent technical material; don't assume domain familiarity without setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out the contribution's significance in Section 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out the contribution's significance in the introduction. Many reviewers stop reading partway through Section 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state what is new and why it matters early; do not bury the main contribution or its significance deeper in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion: reserve for non-obvious insights; include open questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve the conclusion for insights readers couldn't appreciate without prior content. Include open research questions here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many papers the conclusion should add perspective or future directions rather than repeat obvious points; for pure theory papers conclusions are optional unless reviewers expect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct citation commands and follow style
rubrics_metrics.description: Use `\citep{}` and `\citet{}` for proper citation formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the conference's bibliographic conventions so citations render correctly and consistently in the final PDF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use packages that override conference styles (avoid fullpage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the `fullpage` package — overrides conference style files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter official style files or use packages that change layout/formatting required by the venue; this can cause formatting violations or reviewer annoyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose displayed vs inline equations carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose carefully between displayed and inline equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use displayed equations for important or complex expressions to improve readability; keep inline equations for short, simple formulas that don't interrupt flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit theorems to roughly one per paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scattering many named theorems unless each is central; too many theorems can dilute perceived significance and burden the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encapsulate non-trivial arguments as Propositions or Theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Encapsulate non-trivial arguments as Propositions or Theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present important technical claims in formal statements (with proofs deferred or sketched) so reviewers can quickly assess correctness and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: These items form an implicit reviewer rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: These items reflect what Steinhardt-as-reviewer keeps flagging — i.e., they form an implicit reviewer rubric for ML conference papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the listed writing, structure, and technical-presentation points as common reviewer failure modes to avoid; addressing them reduces risk of reviewer critique.
